topics.title: Government vs. Governance and Historical Evolution

concepts.label: Government and Governance: What Is the Difference?
concepts.cardText: In a well-functioning democracy it is not enough to participate only in elections: a robust democracy needs transparent institutions, responsible representatives and the continuous participation of people in public life. Governance in a democratic system is based on transparency, accountability, participation and the rule of law, and places citizens at the centre of the political process, being more people-centric and welfare-oriented. Solving public problems takes much more than a government issuing orders: different institutions and citizens must work together, make decisions, implement them effectively and remain accountable; this process is governance. Government refers to the institutions and authorities that exercise political power (the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary; who governs), while governance refers to the process by which decisions are made, implemented and monitored in the public interest, involving government, citizens, media, civil society and private organisations (how governing is carried out). The government formulates and implements people-centric policies, and good governance ensures they are transparent, accountable, effective and responsive. Street lighting shows the difference: the municipal corporation or panchayat is the government, while governance is the process of planning, implementing and maintaining the lighting with people reporting dark spots and giving feedback.

concepts.label: The Evolution of Governance in India
concepts.cardText: Government is the institutional aspect and governance its functional aspect. The structure of government in India has evolved from historical experiences. Before colonial rulers forced their own models on colonised people, societies governed themselves through local, organic systems; although most colonies became independent by the end of the 20th century, colonial institutions largely persisted. India stands out in two ways: it preserved most of its knowledge of pre-colonial institutions and traditions of governance through texts and practices, and after Independence in 1947 it was not possible to replace all colonial institutions at once, so the leaders framed the Constitution in the spirit of India's own values. Indian institutions continued to draw on traditional ideas: the national motto Satyamev Jayate comes from the Munḍaka Upaniṣhad, and the Supreme Court's motto Yato Dharmastato Jayaḥ comes from the Mahābhārata. Indian tradition has viewed governance as a sacred responsibility rather than merely a means of exercising power: rājadharma, the foremost duty of an ideal king, was to protect the people by upholding Dharma and promote society's welfare, and Gandhi's ideal of Rām Rājya rests on probity, transparency, compassion, welfare and a people-centric orientation.

topics.title: Core Features of Good Governance and E-Governance Tools

concepts.label: Good Governance: Features and Challenges
concepts.cardText: Governance affects daily life: it maintains law and order, protects citizens' rights and freedom, helps people access public services such as education, healthcare and transport, promotes justice and fairness, and builds trust between citizens and government. Governance is the government's responsibility, but good governance depends on how different sections of society and government perform their responsibilities and work together: the government makes laws and provides services, citizens elect representatives, follow the law and participate, the media informs, civil society raises awareness and the private sector brings economic activity and innovation. The features of good governance are responsiveness, transparency, participation, the rule of law, accountability, effectiveness and inclusiveness. Challenges include weak coordination between institutions, unequal access to public services that leaves some groups behind, malpractices and misuse of public office, and misinformation and fake news. Addressing them needs effective institutions, responsible officials, active citizens and continued commitment to good governance principles.

concepts.label: E-Governance: Technology for Better Governance
concepts.cardText: Digital technology has changed the way government interacts with people. E-governance is the use of information and communication technology by governments to provide public services, share information, communicate with citizens, receive feedback and improve administrative processes. It can make governance more transparent, accessible, convenient and quick, substantially reduces paperwork and lets people access services without visiting government offices. It is particularly valuable in a large country like India, enabling governments to deliver services efficiently, transparently, conveniently and quickly across vast geographical areas. Examples of initiatives include UMANG, Aadhaar, GeM (Government e-Marketplace), DigiLocker, CPGRAMS and APAAR. However, e-governance is effective only when people have access to digital devices, reliable internet and the skills to use them, so while technology can strengthen good governance, the government must ensure digital services remain inclusive and accessible to everyone.

topics.title: Public Policy Meaning, Scope and the Policy Cycle

concepts.label: The Meaning of Public Policy and What Makes It 'Public'
concepts.cardText: Public policy is the link between governance and people's needs: it translates governance into planned action by turning public concerns and government priorities into programmes, decisions and solutions. Every day we experience public policies without noticing: roads, traffic signals, clean drinking water, electricity, public parks and waste collection are public services made possible by them. A school's 'Plastic-Free Campus Policy' shows a policy as a planned course of action to solve a problem and achieve a goal. Public policy is a course of action adopted by the government to solve public problems, meet people's needs and promote the welfare of society: it decides what should be done, why, who will do it, how it will be implemented and how success will be measured, and it is monitored and evaluated through a feedback loop. A policy is 'public' when it is made for public benefit, implemented by public institutions and often financed with public money from taxes, addressing issues concerning society as a whole, like education, healthcare, sanitation and public safety. Not every policy is a public policy: a school's phone policy or a company's work-from-home policy applies only to a limited group.

concepts.label: The Policy Cycle and the NEP 2020 Example
concepts.cardText: A public policy is developed through a systematic process rather than a single decision. It begins when citizens, officials, researchers or civil society realise that a new need must be met, a problem resolved or a facility improved. The government then studies the issue, collects information and consults experts, stakeholders and the public. Authorities prepare, review and approve a draft; once approved, it is translated into programmes and schemes giving a framework for ministries, departments and local governments to act. Implementation is continuously monitored and evaluated, with feedback used to improve the policy. Public policy is thus a continuous cycle of problem identification, consultation, policy formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and improvement. The key stages include prioritising (policy desirability), formulation, adoption (framing legislation and regulations), implementation, monitoring and evaluation. The National Education Policy 2020 shows this: a new policy process began in 2015, an expert committee chaired by Dr K. Kasturirangan was set up in 2017, large-scale public consultation reached 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats and gave about 2 lakh suggestions, many incorporated, and the Union Cabinet approved it in July 2020.

concepts.label: Policy, Programmes and Schemes
concepts.cardText: For a policy to be implemented effectively it is organised into programmes and schemes. A policy is a broad goal or direction adopted by the government to address an important public issue; it tells us what the government wants to achieve and why. A programme explains the plan or approach for achieving that goal. A scheme is a specific action or initiative through which the programme is implemented so that its benefits reach the people. In simple terms, policy provides direction, programmes provide the plan, and schemes put the plan into action. For example the National Health Policy 2017 aims at universal access to good quality healthcare, strengthening public healthcare, equity, affordability and accountability, and preventive and promotive care; its programmes include strengthening the healthcare system and digital health information; its schemes include Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, health and wellness centres, Janani Suraksha Yojana and Mission Indradhanush.

concepts.label: Participants in the Public Policy Process
concepts.cardText: Who decides whether new schools are to be built, roads repaired or taxes changed? Not only the government: it takes the combined efforts of many individuals, organisations, officials and ordinary citizens in identifying issues, providing solutions and putting them into action. Citizens identify problems, vote, participate, give suggestions and provide feedback, for example residents requesting a zebra crossing near a school. Elected representatives (MPs, MLAs and local representatives) represent people, raise public issues, take part in law-making and approve budgets. Government officials, departments and ministries at Central, State and local levels prepare and implement policies and programmes, coordinate departments, deliver services and monitor progress, as a district collector does. Civil society organisations, NGOs, experts, researchers and the media study problems, suggest solutions, create awareness, monitor programmes and give feedback. The private sector brings technical know-how, innovation and resources, often working with the government, and international organisations like the WHO bring international experience, technical know-how and financial support.

concepts.label: Policy Coordination and the Role of Citizens
concepts.cardText: Public policymaking and implementation need multi-level planning and decision-making, which is more complex in a vast, diverse country like India. The Khelo Bharat Niti 2025, launched to transform India's sports landscape, shows that a policy's success depends on many stakeholders, each with a role: families supporting their children's sports careers, governments encouraging students, local authorities maintaining grounds, scientists researching nutrition and equipment, and the Central Government providing the policy framework and funding. The Union Government gives the larger framework and funding; states are to build ecosystems (as 'Model Sports States'), host national games and attract private investment through public-private partnerships; districts become 'Model Sports Districts'; blocks organise regular sporting programmes; private organisations sponsor athletes and invest in research. Thus the success of a policy depends on coordination between various stakeholders. Governance is about how decisions are made, implemented and connected to everyday life, and people contribute by voting, following laws, raising concerns, participating in public affairs and giving feedback on services, which helps improve public institutions.

keyPoints.text: Public policymaking and implementation require multi-level planning and decision-making, which becomes more complex and challenging in a country as vast and diverse as India. The government may plan a policy, but its success depends on many stakeholders, and the success of a policy like Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 depends on the coordination between various stakeholders. The Union Government provides the larger policy framework and funding, state governments strengthen sporting ecosystems and host major games and attract private investment through public-private partnerships, and districts and blocks organise sports programmes, while private organisations sponsor sportspersons and invest in research.

checks.criterion: States that policies in a vast, diverse country need multi-level planning and that success depends on coordination among stakeholders, as in Khelo Bharat Niti 2025: the Union provides framework and funding, states build ecosystems and attract private investment, districts and blocks run programmes, and private organisations sponsor and invest.

keyPoints.text: Governance may sound like government, but it is more about how decisions are made, implemented, and connected to people's everyday lives. Elected representatives, government officials, local institutions, civil society organisations, researchers, the media, the private sector, and people all have different but connected roles in good governance. By voting, following laws, raising concerns, participating in public affairs, and giving feedback on government services, people can help improve the way public institutions function. Good governance and public policy are crucial foundations for achieving national development goals.
